newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE- Pakistan election campaign lacks fire.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE- Pakistan election campaign lacks fire.

text.p: For people in Larkana, home of Pakistan's powerful Bhutto clan, elections were festivals to be relished and voting was a near formality.
This year, the atmosphere is different.
Campaigning is low-key and the masses who once gave unstinted support to Benazir Bhutto or her executed father, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, are confused and uncertain.
"I don't know who to vote for," said Mohammad Khan, a worker at the state-owned Larkana Sugar Mills in Naudero.

The mill used to be called the Shahnawaz Bhutto Sugar Mills after Benazir's brother, who died in France of suspected poisoning in 1985. The name was abruptly changed after President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir's government on November 5.
Leghari, once a loyal member of Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP), accused her of allowing corruption, nepotism and other abuses to flourish during her three years in power.
HUSBAND'S LURID REPUTATION
Bhutto's ouster, for the second time in six years, and the lurid reputation of her jailed husband, Asif Ali Zardari, may have shaken her hold on voters in her ancestral land.
Potentially even more damaging than the alleged taint of corruption in her government is the fate of her other brother, Murtaza, who was killed by Karachi police on September 20.
Zardari has been charged with conspiring to murder Murtaza and is awaiting trial in a Karachi jail. Bhutto has denied that he could have had any part in her brother's death.
But some people chanted slogans against the couple when Murtaza's body was brought for burial in the family grave at the village of Garhi Khuda Bux, near Larkana in Sindh province.
Now Murtaza's Lebanese-born widow, Ghinwa, is leading the splinter PPP faction he founded, challenging the main party on its home ground in a move likely to split traditional loyalties.
That could give an opening to the rival Pakistan Muslim League (PML) led by former prime minister Nawaz Sharif.
ECONOMIC CRISIS
The current election mood is also soured by Pakistan's economic crisis. Few candidates can afford to borrow money at interest rates hovering at 20 percent.

"You will not see election carnivals now because of high inflation and a lack of funds," Udham Lal, manager of a Bhutto-owned rice mill opposite her house in Naudero, said as donkey carts hauled freshly harvested rice to the factory gate.
A few small red, black and green PPP flags fluttered on the mud dwellings of Naudero, but the huge party banners that once dominated the rice paddies and guava orchards were gone.
In past elections, the PPP organised blaring cavalcades of ornately decorated cars, buses and trucks packed with flag-waving party workers to help generate enthusiasm.
Petrol prices have been raised at least five times since June, and many candidates are finding that their campaign funds are too thin to lay on the bread and circuses of the past.
On the other hand, it now takes less money to bribe undecided voters, local politicians conceded.
"I could defeat Benazir if I had a million rupees ($25,000)," bragged Ali Mohammad Haqqani, candidate for the religious Jamiat-i-Ulema-i-Islam party.
He is contesting the same seat as Ghinwa Bhutto and her ailing mother-in-law, Nusrat Bhutto, a mainstream PPP candidate.
AUSTERITY

The caretaker government's insistence on austerity has also dampened election enthusiasm. It has barred posters and banners -- and ordered voting for provincial assemblies to be held on the same day as for the National Assembly to cut costs.
"Without a lively campaign, we hardly know if elections are taking place or not," said Hizbullah Morio, owner of the Classic Medical and General Store in Naudero's small and muddy bazaar.
Political analysts in Larkana say holding the polls next Monday bodes ill for the supersitious Bhutto.
Many key events in her life have fallen on Wednesdays.

Her return from exile, the death of her arch-enemy, military ruler General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq, the launch of her first election campaign, her first election win, her first nomination as prime minister, her engagement to Zardari, her wedding day and the birth of her first son -- all happened on Wednesdays.
"Hold the elections on any day except Wednesday and she will not be able to get a majority for the PPP," said a former president of the Larkana Press Club, who asked not to be named.
